left_items.title: The decision
left_items.body: Launch the Carry1st Shop in Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, Colombia and Bolivia by Black Friday, 27 November 2026, through a merchant of record: EBANX direct, or EBANX plus the rails each market needs, through Yuno.

left_items.title: The economics to beat
left_items.body: A $10 average and $5 median ticket, so every fixed fee per transaction is punished; $4 to 5M a month in LatAm by end 2027 (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate).

left_items.title: What EBANX direct gives
left_items.body: One agreement and one integration for all five countries once EBANX enables each; but one approval rate, one price, Bolivia cash only, no MODO.

left_items.title: What is still open
left_items.body: Volumes by country, EBANX's proposed rates, Carry1st's take rate and the tax treatment under each MoR. Every modeled number in this deck carries its label and an owner.

right_cards.title: One integration, every rail Carry1st needs
right_cards.body: EBANX plus any other MoR, acquirer or local method each market needs, all connections on the Yuno SDK: retries and failover across them, Phase 2 without touching checkout.

right_cards.title: A fee that scales with sales, not with transactions
right_cards.body: $7,500 a month including the first $500K of monthly sales, then 40 / 30 / 20 / 10 bps on sales above it. At launch: $7,500 and nothing per transaction; at $4.5M: $21,000 a month, 0.47% of sales.

right_cards.title: A case that pays back in month three
right_cards.body: Base case at run rate: $44.7 per $1,000 of sales through Yuno against $45.0 direct, +$26.7K a month net ($320K a year, 2.3x Yuno's cost); break-even about 68,000 transactions a month.

slides.bottom: EBANX stays at the center and Yuno adds every rail around it; even the conservative case is cost-neutral at run rate.
slides.source: Yuno business-case model, 15 Oct 2026, base scenario: EBANX direct all-in 4.5% of sales and a 15% take rate are estimates, replaced by EBANX's quote and Shop margins. Volumes: Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate.
slides.notes: The whole deck on one slide. Left, where you stand: five markets, six weeks, a $5 median ticket and a run-rate estimate that is yours. Right, what we propose: one integration carrying EBANX plus any other merchant of record, acquirer or local method each market needs, a fee that is a share of what you sell with the first $500K of monthly sales inside the platform fee, and a business case that, in the base scenario, makes the Yuno route the cheaper cost line at run rate before counting approval or coverage gains. Two numbers to keep: break-even at about 68,000 transactions a month, and the conservative case cost-neutral at run rate. Everything modeled is labelled and will be re-cut on your volumes and EBANX's quote.

slides.kicker: WHERE CARRY1ST STANDS · WHAT THE LAUNCH HAS TO GET RIGHT
slides.headline: The Latin America launch has to get five things right, from economics at a $5 ticket to a path to local presence.

items.title: Economics that hold at a $5 to $10 ticket
items.body: Processing savings, higher approval and engineering avoided have to cover the cost of orchestration at small tickets, not only at scale.

items.title: Pricing that scales with sales, not transactions
items.body: With a median ticket near $5, a fixed fee per transaction taxes the core basket; cost should be a share of what the Shop sells.

items.title: One integration for EBANX and any rail added later
items.body: EBANX stays where it is strong; other merchants of record, local acquirers and methods arrive as connections, not new builds.

items.title: A checkout that converts with local methods
items.body: Pix, PSE, SPEI, wallets and QR in local currency, confirming in seconds to match instant top-up delivery.

items.title: A path from merchant of record to local presence
items.body: Launch on a merchant of record now; move country by country to non-resident accounts or local entities later, without a rebuild.

slides.bar: This is our read of what the launch needs; the rest of the deck tests EBANX direct and the Yuno route against these five points.
slides.source: Yuno analysis of the Carry1st Latin America launch, October 2026.
slides.notes: Our read of what the Latin America launch has to get right, in five points. Two are commercial: economics that hold at a small ticket, and a fee that follows sales rather than transactions. One is architectural: EBANX plus whatever else each market needs, without a new build each time. Two are about the gamer and the roadmap: local methods that confirm instantly, and a path to local presence that does not mean rebuilding the checkout. The rest of the deck is built against these five points.

slides.kicker: WHERE CARRY1ST STANDS · THE SHOP AND THE PLAN
slides.headline: Five markets, a $10 average ticket and six weeks to Black Friday: the launch has to be fast, local and cheap per transaction.

tiles.label: storefronts across Africa, the Middle East and the US: game top-ups and gift cards, instant delivery
average ticket; median about $5 (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate)

slides.left_note: Founded 2018 in Cape Town; backed by a16z, BITKRAFT, Google, Konvoy and Sony. Publishing partners include Activision, Supercell and EA. The US storefront already lists Free Fire Diamonds (LATAM) and Brazil SKUs.
slides.mid_header: THE LATAM PLAN AS YOU DESCRIBED IT
mid_items: Brazil first, then Argentina, Mexico, Bolivia and Colombia; all five together if payments, localization and support fit in two to three weeks.
Launch through a merchant of record (no LatAm entities today); non-resident accounts and local entities are a Phase 2 decision.
$4 to 5M a month by end 2027 (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate): about 450,000 transactions a month at a $10 ticket. Volumes by country to come.
slides.right_body: **Live by 27 November 2026.** Local methods that confirm in seconds (Pix, PSE, SPEI, wallets), because the Shop promises instant delivery. **A domestic charge in local currency,** so cards are not declined as cross-border and gamers do not pay FX or foreign-purchase taxes. **One approval rate to beat, not to accept:** a second provider in play from day one. **Spanish and Portuguese** checkout and support. **Costs that scale with a $5 median,** never a fixed fee per transaction.
slides.bar: Six weeks to Black Friday: provider contracts and KYC are the critical path; the Yuno integration itself is measured in days (Yuno estimate).
slides.source: Discovery call, Oct 2026 (Cordel's figures are estimates, not yet aligned internally); shop.carry1st.com sitemap and Carry1st press releases 2021 to 2026, read 15 Oct 2026.
slides.notes: This is the plan as you described it, in your numbers. We label the run rate as your estimate because you told us it is not yet aligned internally, and the model in this deck runs at four volumes so it holds whichever way the alignment lands. The right-hand column is the checklist we built the launch against: speed, local methods that confirm instantly, domestic presentation of the charge, a second provider from day one, and costs that behave at a $5 median.

slides.kicker: WHERE CARRY1ST STANDS · WHAT THE FIVE MARKETS DEMAND
slides.headline: In every launch market the method that wins is local and instant, and most of it sits outside international card rails.

tiles.label: of Brazil's online purchases are Pix (2025); cards 41%
of Colombia's e-commerce transactions run on PSE (Q2 2025)
of Argentina's e-commerce value is in digital wallets (2024)

slides.right_header: WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE SHOP

right_items.title: Instant confirmation is the product
right_items.body: Pix, PSE, SPEI and wallets confirm in seconds, which matches instant top-up delivery. Cash vouchers (Boleto, OXXO, Rapipago) confirm hours or days later and belong in a second wave.

right_items.title: Domestic presentation decides approval
right_items.body: Vendor-reported ranges put cross-border card approval at 30 to 60% against 80 to 90% for local processing (2017 to 2026). A merchant of record charging in local currency is what lets a Brazilian or Mexican debit card approve.

right_items.title: Taxes follow the rail
right_items.body: Argentina adds a 30% perception on foreign-currency card purchases; Brazil charges 3.5% IOF on international card payments. A local-currency charge through the MoR's local entity is domestic for the gamer. TO VALIDATE with each MoR.

right_items.title: Bolivia and Argentina need more than EBANX
right_items.body: EBANX lists only PagosNet cash in Bolivia and no MODO or interoperable QR in Argentina; other providers live on Yuno carry them.

slides.bar: The Shop's African playbook, local methods in local currency, is exactly what LatAm requires; the open question is which rail carries it.
slides.source: Reuters on PCMI data, 10 Feb 2026; CCCE via Valora Analitik, 24 Aug 2025; PCMI 2024 data; AMVO Estudio 2024; approval ranges are vendor-reported (Worldline, Rapyd, Nuvei, Antom, EBANX, 2017 to 2026); ARCA RG 5617/2024; Decree 12.499/2025. PUBLIC DOCS.
slides.notes: Four numbers, one per market, and they point the same way: the winning method is local and it confirms instantly. Pix in Brazil, PSE in Colombia, wallets in Argentina and debit cards in Mexico are the rails the Shop needs on day one. The approval ranges on the right are vendor claims, not independent studies, so we show them as ranges and label them; the direction is not in dispute. The two tax lines explain why a local-currency charge through a merchant of record matters for the gamer, and both are items we will confirm in writing with each merchant of record.

What changes is the integration: the Shop talks to one SDK, every provider is a set of credentials entered as a connection, and routing rules decide which one carries each payment. slides.title: Business case
slides.sub: EBANX direct against EBANX plus local rails through Yuno: four levers, three scenarios, one ticket test
section_list: Appendix: LatAm deep dive and sources
slides.notes: Three slides: the four levers and what each is worth at run rate, the total impact across three scenarios, and why the shape of the fee matters at a $5 median ticket.

slides.kicker: BUSINESS CASE · FOUR LEVERS AT RUN RATE
slides.headline: At $4.5M a month of sales, the four levers are worth about $572K a year to Carry1st in the base case.

levers.name: Processing cost
levers.body: With EBANX and other providers live on the same rails (Pix runs on 27 in Brazil, PSE on 12 in Colombia), volume moves by rule to the cheaper route, and every rate is negotiated against a real alternative. A processing saving is 100% contribution.

levers.name: Integrations avoided
levers.body: A second merchant of record, a local acquirer, a new wallet: built direct, each is 4 to 8 engineering weeks plus 20 to 30% yearly upkeep. On Yuno they are connections already live, switched on from the dashboard, not projects.

levers.name: Approval uplift
levers.body: Direct, every payment goes to one provider. Through Yuno a decline on EBANX retries on a second provider, Monitors reroute on a drop, and routing by BIN and country lifts approval from a 75% baseline. Counted at the take rate, not at face value.

levers.name: Local methods, checkout
levers.body: One checkout returns Pix, PSE, Nequi, SPEI, OXXO, MODO and QR per market, in local currency, so gamers without an international card can pay. Incremental sales are counted at the take rate, net of processing.

slides.assumptions: **Assumptions** All figures in USD, a year, at run rate: 450,000 transactions a month at a $10 average ticket, $4.5M of monthly sales (Carry1st, Cordel, Oct 2026, estimate). Baseline approval 75%; EBANX direct all-in 4.5% of sales (ESTIMATE, replaced by EBANX's quote); 15% take rate on sales (ESTIMATE). Contribution view: L1 and L2 count in full, L3 and L4 at the take rate net of processing. L2: 4 to 8 weeks per integration at $2,000 a week plus upkeep, 24-month equivalent. Ranges are Yuno modelling assumptions, recalibrated on Carry1st's data.
slides.closing: The value can be monetized from launch: Yuno's connections to EBANX and the local rails already exist, so each lever is switched on, not built.
slides.source: Yuno business-case model (bc_model.xlsx), 15 Oct 2026. ESTIMATE; every assumption is on the risks slide in the appendix.
slides.notes: Four levers, two that cut cost and two that add sales. Processing cost comes first because resale margins are thin: with EBANX and other providers live on the same rails, volume moves to the cheaper route by rule, and a saving on processing is worth one hundred cents on the dollar. Integrations avoided is the engineering Carry1st does not spend each time a market needs a new provider. Approval and local methods add sales, and we count them at your take rate, not at face value. The two rows show the conservative and optimistic value of each lever a year at the $4.5M run rate; the base case totals about $572K a year.

right.callout: At launch Carry1st pays the platform fee and nothing per transaction. At the run rate the all-in cost is 0.47% of sales, falling as volume grows.
right.paragraph: Usage on a $5 purchase: $0.020 in tranche 1, $0.005 in tranche 4. A fixed fee stays the same whatever the ticket. The base case returns 2.3x this cost at run rate.

slides.source: Platform fee billed annually. Usage billed monthly in arrears on successful transactions, net 30. Rates locked, tranches reviewed annually as volume grows. All figures in USD.
slides.notes: The proposal in one slide. A flat platform fee of $7,500 a month that already covers the first $500K of monthly sales, and above that a share of what you sell: 40 basis points to $2M, 30 to $5M, 20 to $10M, 10 above, each band on the volume inside it, only on approved payments, never a fee per transaction. At launch you pay the platform fee and nothing else; at the $4.5M run rate the all-in cost is $21,000 a month, 0.47% of sales, under five cents on a $10 purchase. Orchestration, smart routing, Monitors, the vault, the dashboard and a dedicated team are inside the platform fee; network tokens and 3DS are billed on usage and quoted separately.
